strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically important problem: converting off-the-shelf MLLMs into retrievers without costly contrastive fine-tuning, avoiding the massive paired-data requirements of prior post-training approaches.

The three proposed techniques (bypassing the final MLP to alleviate 'lexicalization pressure', controlled-generation prompting with semantic/task/noise priors, and MCQ-based neutral reranking to counter an identified LLM framing effect) are each simple, plug-and-play, and empirically validated via targeted ablations (Tab. 3a-c).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 46 datasets (MMEB + MMEB-V2), multiple MLLM families (Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV) and scales (2B to 32B), demonstrating consistent gains over the training-free E5-V baseline (+33-34%) and strong competitiveness with heavily supervised methods.

The lexicalization-pressure probing analysis is replicated across three model scales (3B/7B/32B) and additional architectures (InternVL, LLaVA, Tab. 5), lending some robustness to the core structural claim, and the framing-effect experiments include reasonable debiasing controls (prompt rephrasing, label-order swapping).

Broader utility is demonstrated beyond benchmark numbers: omni-modal retrieval with Qwen2.5-Omni, unification of retrieval/reranking/generation in a single model, and improved long-video understanding (LVBench) via retrieval-guided frame selection.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (inference cost, dependence on base model quality) and a reproducibility statement with code provided.
weaknesses: The appendix 'theoretical analysis' (Lemma 1) models the final MLP as a linear map (Ah+b), which is not representative of an actual nonlinear MLP, and the proof mainly restates that gradients lie in the span of the LM head rather than rigorously explaining the observed empirical drop in synonym similarity; this weakens the claimed mechanistic justification for removing the final MLP.

No quantitative latency/throughput analysis is provided despite acknowledging that FreeRet incurs substantially higher inference cost than CLIP-style retrievers; the mitigation strategies in Appendix A.5 are only proposed, not empirically demonstrated in this paper.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different backbone architectures and scales across baselines and FreeRet variants, making it harder to cleanly attribute gains to the proposed method versus simply using a stronger/more recent backbone (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL vs Qwen2-VL); a more controlled backbone-matched comparison beyond the single E5-V reproduction would strengthen the causal claims.

The claim of being competitive with the state-of-the-art supervised model is only exactly matched at 7B scale (70.7 vs 70.7) and requires scaling to 32B to clearly surpass, which is a much larger and more expensive model than the compared baselines — the headline claims could be tempered accordingly.

No variance/error bars are reported for the main results or ablations, leaving open questions about the stability of gains, particularly for the framing-effect study where reported accuracy differences (e.g., 5.0%, 8.4%) are based on a single benchmark subset (ImageNet-1K) and may not generalize to other task types.

Individual components draw substantially on existing ideas from the text-embedding literature (PromptEOL-style prompting, calibrate-before-use bias correction for framing effects, layer selection for embeddings), so the core novelty lies primarily in adapting and combining these ideas for the multimodal MLLM retrieval setting rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important question—whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as competitive retrievers without any fine-tuning—and backs it with an unusually extensive empirical sweep: 36 MMEB datasets plus MMEB-V2 video tasks, across many backbone families (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at 3/7/32B, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV, Qwen2.5-Omni).

The 'lexicalization pressure' probing analysis (Fig. 2, replicated across model scales in Fig. 7 and across architectures in Tab. 5) is a genuinely useful diagnostic: it identifies a concrete locus (the final MLP) for degraded embedding quality and the simple fix (dropping it) is validated consistently.

Ablations are reasonably systematic and isolate the contribution of each proposed component: MLP removal (Tab. 3a), controlled-generation prompting (Tab. 3b), and MCQ-based reranking (Tab. 3c, Fig. 4), each showing incremental, plausible gains.

The empirical headline results are striking: training-free FreeRet is shown to outperform heavily trained baselines (GME-7B with 8M pairs, MMRet-7B with 26.2M pairs) and approach/surpass MMEB-supervised SOTA at larger scale, which is a noteworthy and potentially impactful finding if it holds up.

Demonstrations of broader utility (omni-modal retrieval with Qwen2.5-Omni, long-video retrieval-augmented reasoning on LVBench, unification of retrieval/reranking/generation in one model) illustrate the practical versatility of the training-free paradigm beyond the core benchmark numbers.
Code is provided and the prompting/embedding procedures are described in enough detail to support reproduction of the main pipeline.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is in tension with the amount of task-specific prompt engineering used: the 'task alignment' prior requires crafting a bespoke instruction per task/dataset (e.g., 'assess if X is related to topic Y'), and the MCQ reranking template is explicitly stated to be 'adjusted to suit the needs of each task.' This raises the concern that substantial manual/implicit search over prompts on the target benchmark distribution has effectively substituted for gradient-based training, which could inflate reported numbers relative to a truly generic, task-agnostic deployment, and the paper does not report how prompts were selected/validated or whether a held-out set was used to avoid benchmark-specific tuning.

The 'theoretical analysis' in Appendix A.2 (Lemma 1/Corollary) is a rather trivial restatement that cross-entropy gradients lie in the span of the LM head's vocabulary vectors; it does not rigorously model the actual training dynamics (optimizer, residual stream, many update steps, interaction with attention) and so provides only superficial justification dressed in formal notation, overstating the rigor behind the empirical lexicalization finding.

No quantitative efficiency numbers (latency, throughput, FLOPs) are reported anywhere in the main text despite the method's central selling point being 'training-free' deployment; the efficiency discussion is relegated to a qualitative appendix (A.5) that proposes mitigations but never measures the actual overhead relative to CLIP-style or trained MLLM retrievers, undermining claims of practicality at scale.

Backbone scale is a confound in the main comparison: FreeRet is evaluated up to 32B parameters while most supervised baselines use 2B–11B backbones, so part of the reported advantage over trained methods may simply reflect using a much larger, more capable base model rather than the proposed training-free techniques per se; a more controlled comparison (same backbone, with vs. without contrastive fine-tuning) would better isolate the method's contribution.

Results appear to be single-run without error bars or variance reporting, despite known prompt-sensitivity of LLM-based scoring (the framing-effect section itself demonstrates several-point swings from minor wording changes), making it hard to assess the robustness/significance of reported gains.

The reranking stage's benefit (Fig. 5) depends heavily on pool size and quality of the first-stage embedder; its scalability to realistic large-scale retrieval corpora (millions+ candidates) is not empirically demonstrated, only asserted via proposed mitigation strategies in the appendix.

The claimed unification of retrieval/reranking/generation and long-video RAG benefits are demonstrated only qualitatively or on a single benchmark (LVBench, one model), limiting the strength of these broader claims relative to how prominently they are advertised in the abstract and introduction.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important question: whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as strong retrievers without costly post-hoc contrastive fine-tuning, directly tackling a real scalability bottleneck of prior work.

The three technical contributions are conceptually simple but well-grounded in careful empirical analysis: (1) the lexicalization-pressure probing experiment (cosine similarity and LM-head alignment across layers) convincingly localizes where semantic information is lost and is replicated across three model scales (3B/7B/32B) and three model families (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA-OV) in Table 5 and Fig. 7, lending good robustness to the claim; (2) the controlled-generation prompting ablation (Table 3b) cleanly isolates the incremental contribution of each constraint; (3) the framing-effect analysis in reranking is an interesting and underappreciated observation, supported by both context-free bias probing and downstream accuracy correlation.

Extensive empirical validation across 46 datasets (MMEB + MMEB-V2), with the method evaluated on many MLLM backbones and scales, showing consistent and often substantial gains over both training-free (E5-V) and heavily trained baselines (GME, MMRet), and even approaching/surpassing MMEB-supervised SOTA at larger scale.

Good ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice (MLP removal, prompt constraints, label framing, reranking pool size), supporting the claimed mechanisms rather than just reporting end-to-end numbers.

Demonstrates broader utility beyond the core benchmark: omni-modal retrieval with Qwen2.5-Omni, long-video understanding gains on LVBench, and preservation of generative/reasoning abilities, which strengthens the significance argument for a generalist, training-free retrieval paradigm.
Reasonably clear writing, informative figures, and a Reproducibility Statement with code provided.
weaknesses: The appendix 'theoretical analysis' (Lemma 1/Corollary) is informal and does not rigorously establish that h' ≈ P_W(h); it mainly restates the softmax gradient structure and offers intuition rather than a proof that discarding the final MLP preserves more semantic information than it already loses through other mechanisms. This section slightly overclaims rigor it does not deliver.

Efficiency costs of the two-stage, same-model embed+MCQ-rerank pipeline are only briefly acknowledged in the appendix as future mitigation strategies (coarse pre-filtering, candidate pruning, lightweight backbones) rather than empirically measured; no latency/throughput numbers are reported, which limits assessment of real-world deployability at the '100M candidates' scale the paper itself raises.

The controlled-generation prompts (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression) appear to be manually engineered per task category; the paper does not discuss or quantify sensitivity to prompt phrasing/wording variation, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns if the prompts require re-tuning for new domains/tasks not covered by MMEB's four meta-task structure.

The training-free E5-V baseline is self-reproduced, and no independent validation or detailed methodology for ensuring a fully fair comparison (e.g., identical prompt search effort) is given, which could affect the magnitude of the reported +33-34% improvement.

Reported results lack variance/error bars or statistical significance testing across runs, aside from the dedicated probing experiments, making it harder to judge the robustness of some of the larger performance gaps (e.g., in Table 1 and 2).

The omni-modal retrieval capability (Fig. 6) is demonstrated only qualitatively via illustrative examples rather than a quantitative benchmark, so claims of 'natural emergent' omni-modality retrieval are not rigorously substantiated.

While the combination of techniques is effective, each individual idea (discarding a final projection layer, prompt-based embedding control, MCQ-style formatting to reduce label bias) builds closely on prior observations in the LLM embedding and calibration literature (e.g., Li & Zhou 2024; Zhao et al. 2021), somewhat limiting the degree of methodological novelty despite the strong empirical packaging.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: adapting MLLMs to retrieval without costly fine-tuning, directly relevant given the rapid pace of MLLM releases.

Extensive empirical validation across many model families (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at 2B/3B/7B/32B, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV) and benchmarks (MMEB's 36 datasets, MMEB-V2 video tasks, Flickr30K, COCO, cross-lingual MMEB), demonstrating strong generality of the proposed techniques.

The three proposed components (bypassing the final MLP, controlled-generation prompting, MCQ-based reranking) are each supported by targeted probing experiments (Fig. 2, 3, 4) and clean ablations (Tab. 3) that isolate their individual contributions.

Results are compelling: training-free FreeRet is competitive with, and in several cases exceeds, models trained on millions of supervised pairs, which is a notable and useful finding for the community.

Rich supplementary analysis, including a theoretical justification attempt, efficiency/latency comparisons against two-stage trained retrievers (Tab. 9-10), qualitative error analysis, and omni-modal retrieval demonstrations (audio-to-video, image+text-to-video), which strengthen the credibility and practical relevance of the claims.
Honest discussion of limitations regarding inference latency/memory of MLLM-based retrieval and dependence on the base model's inherent quality.
Reproducibility support via a code demo and detailed prompt templates provided in the main text and appendix.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical' justification (Lemma C.1/Corollary C.2) is largely a restatement of the softmax cross-entropy gradient structure and does not rigorously prove that discarding the MLP preserves more task-relevant semantic information; it reads as post-hoc formalization rather than a genuine theoretical contribution.

Individually, the three techniques (layer selection for embeddings, prompt-based control, calibration/format effects for classification) closely mirror known practices in the text-only LLM embedding literature (e.g., PromptEOL, MetaEOL, calibrate-before-use for label bias) discussed in Related Work; the paper's novelty is primarily the systematic transfer and combination of these ideas to the multimodal, two-stage retrieval setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

FreeRet-embed alone (without reranking) does not clearly outperform strong supervised embedders like GME (53.7 vs 56.0 on MMEB), so claims of the embedding stage being competitive should be stated more precisely rather than framed uniformly as outperforming; the large gains rely heavily on the reranking stage.

The MCQ-based reranking stage requires per-candidate forward passes, and while the paper offers mitigation strategies (coarse pre-filtering, controlled candidate counts) in the appendix, scalability to real-world retrieval corpora (hundreds of millions of items) remains a practical concern not empirically demonstrated at scale.

The explanation for the 'LLM framing effect' (pretraining social/pragmatic connotations of Yes/No, Right/Wrong) is plausible but largely speculative; no causal intervention (e.g., controlled fine-tuning or synthetic pretraining ablation) is provided to substantiate the proposed mechanism beyond correlational evidence.

Robustness of the controlled-generation prompts to variations in phrasing is not systematically studied, leaving open whether the method's gains are sensitive to specific wording choices, which is an important reproducibility/robustness consideration for prompt-dependent training-free methods.

Cross-lingual and Flickr30K/COCO generalization experiments use smaller-scale comparisons (e.g., 3B backbone in Table 8) and machine-translated benchmarks, which may introduce their own noise and limit the strength of generalization claims.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning many MLLM backbones (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at multiple scales, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV/OV-1.5) and multiple benchmarks (MMEB, MMEB-V2 video tasks, Flickr30K/COCO, cross-lingual translations, LVBench), which supports the claim of model-agnosticism and broad applicability.
The ablation studies (Tab. 3) cleanly isolate the contribution of each proposed component (MLP removal, controlled prompting, MCQ framing) and show consistent, non-trivial gains across model scales.

The identification of an 'LLM framing effect' in binary reranking (Yes/No vs True/False vs MCQ) is an interesting empirical observation with a plausible explanation tied to pretraining label connotations, and the fix (MCQ framing) is simple and effective.

Thorough supplementary material: efficiency analysis against two-stage baselines, error analysis with illustrative failure cases, and discussion of scalability strategies for massive candidate pools, which aids practical understanding.
Addresses a practically relevant problem: avoiding costly contrastive fine-tuning and large paired-data curation for every new MLLM backbone or modality combination.
weaknesses: The three 'advances' are individually fairly well-established ideas repackaged with new terminology: skipping the final projection layer before the LM head for embeddings is a known trick in the LLM-embedding literature (cited works like MoEE, PromptEOL already explore hidden-state choices), structured/constrained prompting for better summarization is standard prompt engineering, and framing binary judgments as multiple-choice to reduce label bias is a known calibration technique (the paper itself cites Zhao et al. 2021 'Calibrate before use' as the origin of this diagnosis). The novelty is thus mostly in combination and application to the multimodal retrieval setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The appendix 'theoretical analysis' (Lemma C.1/Corollary C.2) is a trivial restatement that softmax cross-entropy gradients lie in span(W); it does not rigorously establish that semantic information is preserved or that the orthogonal component is actually meaningful/semantic rather than noise, so framing it as formal justification is somewhat overstated.

Despite being branded 'training-free,' the method relies on carefully hand-crafted, task-specific prompts (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression instructions, and per-task MCQ option wording), which function as a lightweight form of manual tuning against the target benchmark (MMEB). The degree of prompt engineering needed to reach reported numbers is not fully transparent in the main text, raising reproducibility and fairness-of-comparison concerns relative to 'zero-shot' claims.

Reranking cost scales with candidate pool size and becomes substantially more expensive at higher r (e.g., r50 latency ~2.97s vs 0.08s for embedding-only in Table 10), which somewhat undercuts the 'efficient, lightweight' framing, though this is acknowledged in the limitations.

The efficiency comparison in Table 9 is not fully apples-to-apples: baselines (MM-Embed, LamRA) use two separate 7B models for embedding and reranking while FreeRet reuses a single model, which mechanically favors FreeRet's reported memory/latency without necessarily reflecting a fundamental methodological advantage.

Generalization claims beyond MMEB are relatively thin: the broader multimodal embedding benchmark MIEB mentioned in related work (as evidence that training-based methods overfit to MMEB) is never actually tested with FreeRet to substantiate the implied superior cross-benchmark generalization.

Some reported results are only roughly competitive with, not clearly superior to, top supervised methods (e.g., FreeRet 70.7 vs UniME-V2 69.6 is a narrow margin, and several embedding-only numbers trail supervised approaches), so the 'substantially outperforms' framing in the abstract is an overstatement in places.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem (training-free MLLM-based retrieval) with a clean plug-and-play framework, avoiding costly contrastive fine-tuning for every new backbone/modality.

Each of the three contributions (bypassing the final MLP, controlled embedding generation, MCQ-based reranking) is backed by targeted probing/diagnostic experiments (layer-wise cosine similarity, synonym/antonym/random word-pair analysis, context-free label-bias analysis) rather than being proposed purely heuristically.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical validation: results on MMEB (36 datasets) and MMEB-V2 video tasks show FreeRet is competitive with or exceeds models trained on millions of pairs, and ablations (Tab. 3) isolate the contribution of each design choice cleanly.

Good generalization evidence: experiments span multiple MLLM families and scales (Qwen2-VL/2.5-VL at 2B-32B, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV), and appendices add cross-lingual MMEB translations, standard Flickr30K/COCO benchmarks, long-video (LVBench) results, and omni-modal retrieval demonstrations (audio-to-video, image+text-to-video), which together strengthen the generality claims beyond the main benchmark.

Reasonably transparent treatment of practical concerns: a computational efficiency analysis (latency/memory vs. baselines and vs. number of reranked candidates), an explicit limitations section, and an error analysis identifying concrete failure modes (missed implicit relational cues, visual-similarity bias) add credibility and reproducibility value.
Code demo is provided, aiding reproducibility of a method that otherwise depends on many small prompt-design choices.
weaknesses: The appended 'theoretical analysis' (Appendix C) is a loose plausibility argument (gradient lies in span of LM head vectors) rather than a rigorous proof that discarding the final MLP preserves more semantic information; it does not formally quantify information loss or guarantee improvement, and this framing could be stated more modestly.

The core idea of extracting embeddings from an intermediate/pre-final layer rather than the final lexical layer echoes similar observations in prior training-free text-embedding work (e.g., layer-wise analyses in MetaEOL, MoEE); the paper's novelty is largely in applying and validating this within MLLMs, which is useful but somewhat incremental relative to the framing as a new 'advance.'

The explanation of the LLM framing effect (social/pragmatic connotations of words like Yes/No/Right/Wrong) is plausible but remains correlational; no causal intervention isolates pretraining corpus bias as the mechanism versus other confounds (e.g., tokenization or calibration effects already studied by Zhao et al. 2021).

Pointwise MCQ reranking still requires one full forward pass per query-candidate pair, and per Table 9/10 latency grows substantially with candidate count (e.g., 0.08s to ~3s per sample at 50 candidates); the proposed mitigations for massive-candidate (100M+) scenarios in Appendix F are only qualitative suggestions without empirical validation at that scale, so true large-scale deployability remains unproven.

Prompt designs (task-alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression phrasing) appear to have been refined using MMEB itself, raising some concern about possible implicit tuning to this benchmark's idiosyncrasies, even though supplementary Flickr30K/COCO and cross-lingual results partially mitigate this concern.

Main result tables do not report variance/error bars across prompt rephrasings or sampling, despite the paper's own findings that generation is sensitive to small prompt/framing changes, which could affect confidence in the reported margins over baselines.
